Calm isn’t taught—it’s engineered! Moving your dog from a high-arousal state (barking, pulling, or overstimulation) to a regulated, relaxed state comes down to changing their brain state, not just their behavior. 
By starting with baseline exercises like capturing calm, mat training, and practicing impulse control, you help lower stress levels and set your pup up for success! 🐾🎯

See this little lead ? This is a training lead, and no it’s not for recall or loose lead training 🐾

But rather something we can use indoors to help prevent unwanted behaviours, boost our puppies confidence around handling and guide them whilst they learn to navigate their new home 🏠 

🩵 Is your puppy jumping on your furniture becoming an issue? This lets us gently guide them off and reinforce where we want them to be.

💛Is your puppy nervous around you handling them? This lets us manage them without overstepping their boundaries and breaking their trust in you.

🩵Is your puppy just being an absolute pickle and getting up to mischief! Possibly excessively mouthing (what I like to call shark mode 🤣) or stealing everything in sight? This lets us remove them from the situation and redirect their behaviour.

💛Is your puppy jumping up at your guests or trying to rush out the front door every time it opens? This lets us prevent rehearsal of this behaviour and teach the dog what we want them to do instead. 

The lead is there to make your intervention as smooth as possible making sure to not cause more worry for your puppy which over handling often does or adding to excitement. It’s there to help you manage situations, prevent unwanted behaviours and provide opportunity to teach them what we want to see instead ☺️

Please remember to always supervise your puppy when using an indoor lead and make sure to remove it when there alone to prevent any injury 🙂

Ever wondered why your dog can absolutely nail something at home, then seemingly forget the whole thing the moment you step outside?

They haven’t forgotten. The real world is simply a much harder classroom.

At home, there might be very little competing for your dog’s attention. Head outside and suddenly there are people, other dogs, traffic, unfamiliar places, exciting smells and approximately eleventy-billion things demanding immediate investigation.
That’s why training for real life takes practice.

Start somewhere your dog can succeed, introduce distractions gradually and use rewards that genuinely matter to them. Once a skill is going well, practise it in the places you’ll actually want to use it.

And remember, useful training looks different for every dog and every household.

Maybe you’d love easier walks, better recall, calmer café visits or a dog who can settle while you stop for a chat.

Everything Dog’s 1:1 training gives you the chance to focus on the skills that will make a genuine difference to everyday life with your dog.

Because the best training is training you can actually use.

Why the harness has to go.

Harnesses were invented for huskies pulling sleds. They are engineered to let a dog lean in and pull.

Then we strap one on a Labrador and wonder why they drag us down the pavement.

They can quietly damage your dog's body — altered gait, muscular compensation, premature arthritic change. Front-clip "no-pull" harnesses are worse.

They kill communication. A flat collar lets you talk through feather-light signals. A harness connects you to a lump of nylon in the middle of their back. No conversation. Just a tow rope.

And here is the quiet damage most owners never see: once your dog decides they're in charge of the walk, why would they not also run the door, the sofa, the postman, the whole house?

The walk is the clearest moment of leadership your dog has in their day. Don't hand it over.

Your walk should be the best part of your day. You and your dog. Side by side. One team.

Has your dog ever suddenly charged towards another dog? Or have you been walking with a friend when your dog’s reaction turned a manageable encounter into something much more serious?

Perhaps it happened for the first time and caught you completely off guard. Perhaps it’s become a pattern, and you now choose quiet routes to avoid other dogs altogether.

It can be reassuring to think, “But they’re fine with my friends’ dogs.” However, getting along with familiar dogs doesn’t necessarily mean your dog can cope with unfamiliar ones.

Choosing quieter walks can be a sensible part of managing things, but unexpected encounters still happen. That’s why understanding your dog’s behaviour, taking precautions and working on those difficulties matters.

There’s a legal responsibility here too. Under the Dangerous Dogs Act 1991, it is an offence to allow a dog to be dangerously out of control. A dog doesn’t have to bite someone for this to apply—behaviour that gives someone reasonable grounds to fear being injured can be enough.

Having a dog who struggles around other dogs doesn’t make you a bad owner. But taking steps to keep your dog and those around them safe is essential.

At Val’s K9 Training, I can help you understand what’s behind those reactions, recognise the early signs and develop practical skills to manage encounters and reduce the risk of escalation.

You don’t have to figure it all out alone—but please don’t wait for a serious incident before seeking support. 🐾

🤭 Feeling the wind in my ears 🤭

This walk was a very strange one. As soon as we parked up we saw a farmer with around 5 Beagles being exercised the way that we originally wanted to go so we chose to go in the opposite direction hoping that meant we had a safe walk without seeing anything...

During that walk we could hear the Hunt horn in the distance so obviously they were following that. 

Now, on the way back to the car we were at the brow of a hill when we suddenly saw that same farmer but this time with around at least 50 Beagles running in the same field as us. Mum panicked and we quickly moved to the other side of the field so we had bushes between us. Obviously these Beagles are working dogs and chances are they wouldn't interact with us but the effect it would have on me when I'm really not a fan of oncoming dogs especially when they're off lead, we needed to create that distance. 

We did, and I looked and chose not to react!!! Big win for me! 🥰

A few weeks back I posted about the feelings and emotions I felt after loosing Prince. And off the back of that I got a lot of you asking about how we managed Prince's reactivity. And to be honest I find it hard to try and give advice on the subject as there isn't a one size fits all answers. Every dog is completely different and I think it differs hugely between small and large breeds. For example, what I talk about in this post I would imagine to be pretty tough on a bigger, more 'athletic' dog- I'm completely aware that not everyone will be able to relate to 'never walking there dog again' as for some breeds this just wouldn't be suitable. But this is our story, this was our journey. In the last quarter half of his life Prince was essentially a little house dog. Every now and again we'd take him to a private field or if the weather was bad I'd take him somewhere I knew we wouldn't see anyone but it was never really worth it. He was happiest at home so that's where he stayed ❤️‍🩹
